title: The Fisherman and the Sprat
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Fisherman cast his net into the sea, and when he drew it up again it contained nothing but a single Sprat that begged to be put back into the water. "I'm only a little fish now," it said, "but I shall grow big one day, and then if you come and catch me again I shall be of some use to you." But the Fisherman replied, "Oh, no, I shall keep you now I've got you: if I put you back, should I ever see you again? Not likely!"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fisherman's net contain when he draws it up?
options: A large catch of many fish
An old boot and some seaweed
Nothing but a single Sprat
Two small fish tangled together

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Sprat beg the Fisherman to do?
options: Put it back into the water
Sell it at the market instead
Give it to a hungry seabird
Throw it back with the rest of the net

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Sprat promise about its future size?
options: That it will never grow any larger
That it will bring other fish to the net
That it will guide the Fisherman to a better spot
That it shall grow big one day

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Sprat say will happen if the Fisherman catches it again later?
options: It will already belong to someone else
It shall be of some use to him
It will be too big for his net
It will have moved to a different sea

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fisherman decide to do with the Sprat?
options: Release it as it requested
Trade it for a larger fish
Keep it now that he has it
Give it to another fisherman

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Fisherman doubt he would catch the Sprat again if he released it?
options: The sea is too vast to guarantee finding the same fish twice
The Sprat has already tricked him once before
He believes the Sprat is lying about growing bigger
He plans to stop fishing in that spot altogether

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Fisherman's choice suggest about weighing a certain gain against an uncertain future one?
options: He always prefers to wait for a larger prize
He values the Sprat's word more than his own judgment
He is indifferent to the size of his catch
He prefers the small certain gain over the bigger, uncertain promise

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "cast" mean in "cast his net into the sea"?
options: To carefully fold something up
To throw or fling something out
To repair something that is broken
To count something one by one

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "Sprat" refer to in the passage?
options: A type of fishing net
A wooden fishing boat
A small kind of fish
A tool used to mend nets

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: A sure thing in hand is often preferred over an uncertain promise later
Fishermen should always release the fish they catch
Small fish are more valuable than large ones
Promises made by animals cannot be trusted

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fisherman do with his net at the start?
options: He mends a tear in it
He lays it out to dry
He sells it to another fisherman
He casts it into the sea

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Sprat describe its current size?
options: "I'm already the biggest fish here"
"I'm only a little fish now"
"I'm too weak to be worth keeping"
"I'm the last of my kind in these waters"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what final word does the Fisherman use to close his reply?
options: "Perhaps another day"
"We shall see"
"Not likely!"
"I promise to think it over"

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what is the Sprat trying to convince the Fisherman of?
options: That it will be more valuable to him if released now and caught later
That it is not actually edible in its current state
That another fisherman already claimed it first
That it can help him catch more fish immediately

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Fisherman's answer be considered practical rather than unkind?
options: He genuinely dislikes all small fish on principle
He has already promised the Sprat to someone else
He believes the Sprat is trying to escape permanently
He has no guarantee the same fish could be found again later

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Sprat "begged" to be released?
options: It demanded angrily
It pleaded earnestly
It joked playfully
It hinted quietly

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Fisherman throws back every fish he catches that day
A Sprat convinces the Fisherman to release it unharmed
A Fisherman keeps a small fish rather than trust its promise of future value
A Fisherman catches many fish besides the Sprat
